title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a training-data sourcing decision made before any product reached users. Suno reportedly admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files available on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the sources. That data collection happened upstream of the generation system itself, meaning every song the system later produced carried the legal exposure embedded at the training stage. The failure was not in the model's outputs in isolation but in the absence of any rights-clearance process applied to the input data before training began.

The deployment-stage symptom is that the system could reproduce recognizable versions of specific copyrighted recordings when given targeted prompts. That reproducibility is what made the infringement allegation concrete and demonstrable in court: plaintiffs could submit generated audio alongside originals as evidence. A rights-audit of training data before model deployment, or filtering to exclude copyrighted material, would have been the point at which this exposure could have been addressed, though whether such measures are technically sufficient is not established.

What is not established is that any court has made a final determination of liability applicable to all parties: one German court ruled against Suno in a case brought by GEMA, some lawsuits ended in settlements rather than verdicts, and other cases including class actions and suits by independent artists and music publishers remained in progress. Settlements with Warner Music Group and Universal Music involve licensing arrangements, but the terms and their implications for ongoing liability are not fully detailed in the reporting.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits argue that the companies deliberately concealed what music they used for training and that their business model is fundamentally based on copyright infringement.

As evidence, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by using specific prompts in both AI generators. They submitted examples showing the AI outputs closely mirrored songs by artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Chuck Berry, Mariah Carey, and Green Day. The labels provided a thumb drive of AI-generated music allegedly copying originals and submitted a list of thousands of specific copyrighted works they claim were scraped. The companies are being sued in New York and Massachusetts, and the case will establish important legal precedent for how generative AI services must handle copyright protection.
